paras: The lynching of J. J. Dickison Jr. was the killing of a prisoner held for an alleged murder at the Sumter county jail in Leesburg, Florida, reported in October 1881 as having occurred some two months earlier. The case drew notice because the victim's father, General Dickerson, set out to identify the lynchers and prosecute them as murderers. A grand jury indicted the jail's guards for manslaughter but failed to identify the lynchers.

Dickison, called "young Dickerson" and the son of General Dickerson "of Georgia," was in the Leesburg jail on a charge of "an alleged murder," the victim of which the reports do not name. His race is not stated in any of the reports.

According to a Columbus, Georgia, dispatch of October 6, Dickison was "taken from the jail" and lynched. Florida reports instead placed the lynching "in the prison of Sumter county," and none of the reports gave a date, time or method. A Black prisoner held in the jail at the same time escaped, or in the Tallahassee Economist's words was "allowed to escape."

General Dickerson captured the escaped prisoner, who was lodged in the Ocala jail and gave the names of several men implicated. The Economist reported that D. S. Walker Jr. had left for Leesburg as the general's attorney "to ferret out and prosecute to the utmost." By October 21 the grand jury had indicted H. B. Marawether, Hotcher, Sherill and a fourth man, who had been guarding the jail, for manslaughter in the fourth degree. The same column reported that the grand jury had "utterly failed to find out" who the lynchers were, and no report of a trial was found.

The Columbus wire ran on October 7 in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier under "Lynchers to Feel the Law" and in the Omaha Daily Bee under "LYNCHED FOR ALLEGED MURDER." Both printings stressed that the general was "a man of wealth and influence" who meant to see the lynchers "punished as murderers." The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer carried a shorter version the same day.

Closer to the scene, the Savannah Morning News reported the prosecution and the grand jury's failure in brief items within its "Florida Affairs" digest, alongside railway and orange-crop news and without comment.

The Georgia wire said Dickison was taken from the jail, while the Florida items said he was killed in it. The Florida items came through the Tallahassee Economist and Florida court news, closer to the scene than the Columbus report.

bases: A prisoner held for an alleged murder was taken from or killed in the Sumter county jail by unnamed 'parties' and 'lynched' (A1, A2, A4, A5).

The papers report that Dickison was lynched in or taken from the county jail while held for an alleged murder, by 'parties' among whom 'several men' were named as implicated (A1, A2, A4, A5); his father sought to have the lynchers punished as murderers (A2, A4).
A Florida report relayed from the Tallahassee Economist (A1, A5) and a separate Columbus, Georgia, wire (A2, A4) agree that General Dickerson's son was lynched at the Sumter county jail.

accounts.label: Florida report (Tallahassee Economist via Savannah)
accounts.gist: Dickerson's son was lynched in the Sumter county prison; the Black fellow prisoner was 'allowed to escape', was captured and named lynchers; counsel was sent to prosecute.

accounts.label: Columbus, Ga., wire
accounts.gist: The son of General Dickerson of Georgia was taken from the Leesburg jail and lynched for an alleged murder; a Black prisoner escaped, was recaptured and named several men; the father vowed to have them punished as murderers.

accounts.label: Florida court news (Savannah)
accounts.gist: The jail guards were indicted for fourth-degree manslaughter, but the grand jury failed to find out who the lynchers were.

framing.detail: Northern and western papers ran the Columbus wire as a crime brief, the New Haven paper under 'Lynchers to Feel the Law' and the Omaha Bee under 'LYNCHED FOR ALLEGED MURDER', stressing the father's wealth and his aim to punish the lynchers as murderers.
The Savannah Morning News carried the case as items in its 'Florida Affairs' digest among railway and orange-crop notes, reporting the prosecution and the grand jury's failure without comment.
